changed.old_text: Existentialism is a loose family of ideas, not a tidy school. It starts from life as a person lives it, not from a detached viewpoint. Its central idea is that we are not born with a fixed nature. We make ourselves through our choices, and we are responsible for who we become. Two nineteenth-century thinkers laid the groundwork: Kierkegaard, from Denmark, and Nietzsche, a German philosopher. In mid-twentieth-century France, Sartre and Beauvoir made it famous.

One of its core ideas is that we make ourselves through our choices, and we are responsible for who we become. Two nineteenth-century thinkers laid the groundwork: Søren Kierkegaard, from Denmark, and the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche. It became famous in mid-twentieth-century France through Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir, two French philosophers who also wrote novels.

changed.old_text:
Being authentic means being true to yourself. Existentialists criticise living by rules and expectations we pick up from others. As Heidegger put it, we enjoy, read and judge things as 'they' do. Doing what everyone does is comforting, because it feels like living well. But it hides our freedom from us. Sartre and Beauvoir call this self-deception 'bad faith'. I am in bad faith when I treat myself as a fixed thing: 'I am what I am'. I am also in bad faith when I pretend my situation puts no limits on my choices. Several thinkers had a name for the crowd we drift with:
- Kierkegaard: 'the public'
- Nietzsche: 'the herd'
- Heidegger: 'the They'
changed.new_text:
Being authentic means being true to yourself. Existentialists criticise our habit of living by the rules and expectations of everyone around us. Heidegger's name for this crowd was 'the They'. We enjoy, read and judge things as 'they' do. It feels like living well, but it hides our freedom from us. So we are deceiving ourselves. Sartre and Beauvoir call this self-deception 'bad faith'. It comes in two forms:
- Treating yourself as a fixed thing: 'I am what I am', and nothing can change me.
- Pretending you have no limits, as if your past and your situation did not constrain your choices.

- Heidegger: 'resoluteness', a focused grip on your chosen path that stays open to letting it go.
- Sartre and Beauvoir: seeing your unsettled situation clearly, accepting it, and taking responsibility for what you do.

changed.old_text: As nineteenth-century Europe became less religious and more scientific, the old religious picture that gave life moral direction began to collapse. Nietzsche diagnosed the result: nihilism, the shocking sense that our existence has no overall reason or purpose. His image for this loss was 'the death of God'. The French novelist Albert Camus called our situation 'the absurd'. It is the clash between our 'wild longing for clarity' and 'the unreasonable silence of the world'. Yet this need not end in despair. For Camus, the absurd calls for action, not suicide. Beauvoir held that existence is not absurd but ambiguous: its meaning is never fixed, so we keep making it.
changed.new_text: As nineteenth-century Europe became less religious and more scientific, the old religious picture that gave life moral direction began to collapse. Nietzsche diagnosed the result: nihilism, the shocking sense that our existence has no overall reason or purpose. His image for this loss was 'the death of God'. The French novelist Albert Camus called our situation 'the absurd'. It is the clash between our 'wild longing for clarity' and 'the unreasonable silence of the world'. Camus asked whether such a life is worth living. His answer was yes: the absurd calls for action, not suicide. Beauvoir insisted that existence is not absurd but 'ambiguous'. Calling it absurd, she said, denies that it can ever be given a meaning. Calling it ambiguous says 'its meaning is never fixed', so we keep making it.

changed.old_text:
Sartre and Beauvoir argued that we see ourselves through 'the look' of others. Their gaze can turn us into objects. Relationships then become a power struggle. Sartre's play No Exit sums this up in its famous line that hell is other people. But there is a better way. Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other person's freedom instead of possessing them. She and Sartre concluded that wanting my own freedom commits me to wanting it for others. In Beauvoir's words, to will oneself free is also to will others free. Later, Sartre shifted his focus from the single person to society. Three things pushed him:
- the Nazi occupation of France
- his own time as a prisoner of war
- attacks on his ideas from Marxist critics
changed.new_text: Sartre and Beauvoir argued that we see ourselves through 'the look' of others. Their gaze can turn us into objects. Relationships then become a power struggle. Sartre's play No Exit sums this up in its famous line that hell is other people. But there is a better way. Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other person's freedom instead of possessing them. Why does my freedom need yours? If I value my own freedom, I must also want it for others. As Sartre put it, in wanting freedom 'we discover that it depends entirely on the freedom of others'.

changed.old_text: Existentialism is not only atheist. Kierkegaard was a Christian. He prized 'a truth which is true for me', lived and felt rather than proved. His book Fear and Trembling retells the Bible story in which God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. Abraham becomes a 'knight of faith': someone who commits to a truth that reason cannot make sense of. He 'leaps' into a paradox, alone with a choice no one else understands. The Jewish thinker Martin Buber stressed meeting another person as a 'You', a whole person. The opposite is treating them as an 'It', a thing to use. Nietzsche and Sartre, by contrast, saw God as irrelevant or even harmful to our deepest choices.
changed.new_text: Existentialism is not only atheist. Kierkegaard was a Christian. He prized 'a truth which is true for me', lived and felt rather than proved. His book Fear and Trembling retells the Bible story in which God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. Here is the paradox. As a father, Abraham has a moral duty to protect his son. God's command asks him to break that duty. By committing to God's command, Abraham becomes a 'knight of faith': someone who puts a personal truth above ordinary morality, a truth reason cannot make sense of. Nietzsche and Sartre, by contrast, saw God as irrelevant or even harmful to our deepest choices.

changed.old_text:
Early hints of this outlook go back to ancient philosophy and to later writers on death and the meaning of life. But the ideas became a movement only in the nineteenth century. Religion's hold was fading, and industry and bureaucracy made society feel impersonal. Early voices included:
- Kierkegaard, who attacked the philosopher Hegel's system of all reality for leaving out the single living person.
- Nietzsche, who foresaw the coming nihilism.
- The Russian novelist Dostoevsky, whose 'underground man' refuses to be reduced to 'a piano key' in a world run by fixed laws.
changed.new_text:
Existentialism became a movement in the nineteenth century, as industry and bureaucracy made society feel impersonal. Early voices included:
- Kierkegaard, who attacked detached philosophy for leaving out the single living person.
- Nietzsche, who foresaw the coming nihilism.
- The Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky. His 'underground man' refuses to be reduced to 'a piano key' by the view that laws of cause and effect decide everything a person does.

changed.old_text:
In the twentieth century, German thinkers such as Husserl, Jaspers and Heidegger laid more groundwork. They gave the movement its roots in phenomenology: the study of how we experience the world from our own point of view. Heidegger's book Being and Time (1927) shaped Sartre and Beauvoir. The movement then exploded in France in the middle of the century. Sartre's Being and Nothingness appeared in 1943, the year the French thinker Gabriel Marcel coined the word 'existentialism'. Its backdrop was:
- the Second World War
- the Nazi death camps
- the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
changed.new_text:
In mid-twentieth-century France, its backdrop was the Second World War, the Nazi death camps and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Three dates mark its rise:
- 1927: Heidegger's Being and Time, which shaped Sartre and Beauvoir.
- 1943: Sartre's Being and Nothingness. The word 'existentialism' is first used.
- 1945 to 1949: Sartre's lecture Existentialism Is a Humanism and Beauvoir's The Second Sex.

changed.old_text: Who counts as an existentialist is disputed. The word names no single set of beliefs. Most thinkers grouped under it never used it, or rejected it. Only Sartre and Beauvoir openly claimed it. In 1947 Heidegger rejected any link between his thought and Sartre's existentialism. Yet both encyclopedias we draw on, Stanford's and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, still count him as a key figure. Camus gave a 1945 interview titled, in English, 'No, I am not an existentialist'. Even so, the Stanford encyclopedia places his essay The Myth of Sisyphus squarely in the tradition.
changed.new_text: The label 'existentialist' is itself disputed. Of the major figures, only Sartre and Beauvoir openly claimed it. Heidegger and Camus both rejected it. Even so, scholars still place both within the tradition. Some argue the label does more harm than good, because it lumps very different ideas together.

changed.old_text: In Germany, critics such as Adorno called existentialism obscure, abstract and even mystical, Heidegger above all. Many other philosophers agreed. After Marxist criticism in the 1940s and 1950s, Sartre himself decided his early idea of 'radical' freedom, made by choice alone, was too abstract. It ignored the social conditions that limit real choices. The French philosopher Merleau-Ponty objected that no one is free apart from other people and history. Later French thinkers faulted Sartre for neglecting language and the impersonal structures that shape meaning.

changed.old_text: Sartre's own example is a student of his in wartime France. The student's brother had been killed in the German attack of 1940. He could go to England and fight with the Free French Forces. Or he could stay with his mother, who lived only for him. He came to Sartre for advice. But choosing an adviser, Sartre said, is already a choice: you more or less know what they will say. His only reply was 'You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent.' One way to use his point: before your next hard choice, ask yourself why you picked the person you are asking, and what you already expect them to say.

A 2015 review pooled the results of 15 trials of existential therapies. Meaning-focused therapies had large effects on people's sense of meaning. It found most support for structured programmes that discussed meaning directly with physically ill patients. But the studies were few and low in quality.
